segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus was led up into the wilderness by the Spirit, to be tested by the devil.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the tempter came up and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If you are the Son of God, tell these stones to become loaves of bread.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is written: ‘A person shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes out through the mouth of God.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the devil took him to the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down; for it is written: ‘He will command his angels concerning you, and on their hands they will lift you up, so that you will not strike your foot against a stone.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Again it is written: ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Again the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go away, Satan! For it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the devil left him, and look, angels came and waited on him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And leaving Nazareth, he went and settled in Capernaum by the sea, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles—

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: the people sitting in darkness have seen a great light, and on those sitting in the region and shadow of death a light has dawned.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From then on Jesus began to proclaim and say,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Turn back, for the kingdom of the heavens has come near.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Come, follow me, and I will make you fishers of people.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once they left their nets and followed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once they left the boat and their father and followed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went around all of Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every ailment among the people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: News of him spread throughout all Syria, and they brought to him all who were ill, those suffering from various diseases and severe pains, those possessed by demons, those who had seizures, and the paralyzed, and he healed them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And large crowds followed him from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan.

notes.note: Most translations have “tempted” here. The Greek verb means to put to the test, and in the Greek Old Testament it is the regular word for God testing Israel in the wilderness, the background this scene draws on. Modern “tempt” has narrowed to enticing someone to sin, which hides that link; lexicons recognize both senses, and which fits best here is disputed. The same verb lies behind “the tempter” in verse 3, and a compound of it behind “put to the test” in verse 7.

All three of Jesus’ replies come from Deuteronomy 6–8 (8:3; 6:16; 6:13), where Moses looks back on Israel’s forty years of testing in the wilderness. A reader who knew the Scriptures would have heard Jesus’ forty days as a reliving of that story. The devil’s own quotation in verse 6 is from Psalm 91:11–12.

The Greek word was used for a projecting edge or tip, and here names some high point of the temple complex; exactly which part is unknown. The traditional “pinnacle” is kept, though a spire should not be imagined. Suggestions include a corner of the outer wall above the Kidron valley or the edge of the sanctuary roof.

The verb’s everyday sense is to attend to someone’s needs, especially by serving food, which fits the end of a forty-day fast. “Ministered” now sounds religious and vague. “Served” was avoided only because it has just been used in verse 10 for a different Greek verb meaning religious service to God.

Most translations say John was “arrested” or “put in prison.” The Greek verb simply means to hand someone over into another’s power, and Matthew uses the same word later for what happens to Jesus and what will happen to his disciples. Rendering it the same way throughout lets the reader see that chain. The imprisonment itself is described in Matthew 14:3.

One Greek word means both “nations” and, in the plural, the non-Jewish peoples; this translation renders it “Gentiles” or “nations” according to sense, and “Galilee of the nations” is also possible here. The quotation is from Isaiah 9:1–2, which speaks of northern territories that fell early to Assyrian conquest.

“Repent” is the traditional rendering, and most translations keep it as an established term that includes a change of life. In current English, though, the word centers on feeling sorry. The Greek carries the prophets’ call to “return” to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct, which “turn back” conveys.

The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase characteristic of Matthew, and a first-century hearer would have noticed it. Most translations flatten it to “the kingdom of heaven.” The phrase is generally taken as equivalent to “the kingdom of God” in the other Gospels.
The Greek word means human beings in general, not males, so “people” is more accurate than the traditional “men.” The phrase plays on “fishermen” in the previous verse, which is the same Greek noun.

“Gospel” has become a religious term or a book title. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, also used of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations already alternate between “good news” and “gospel.”

The Greek word is built on the word for “moon” and reflects the ancient belief that the moon caused the condition. In Matthew 17:15 the same word describes a boy who falls into fire and water, so recurring seizures are in view. Many modern versions have “epileptics”; “seizures” describes the symptoms without importing a modern diagnosis.

Ranges from serving at table to ministry in general, and must be kept distinct from δουλεύω and λατρεύω, which also attract “serve.”
Recurs across the Gospels, and “demon-possessed,” “demonized” and “afflicted by demons” imply different things about the condition.
Extremely frequent; translators vary between “behold,” “look,” “suddenly” and omitting it, so a single policy is needed for uniformity.
Versions alternate between “wilderness,” “desert” and “deserted place,” and the Exodus echo depends on a consistent rendering.
